implementation_notes: The tolerance comes from document navigation rather than from binding: nlohmann::json::value(key, default_value) is documented as the equivalent of Python's dict.get(key, default) and returns the default when the key is absent (without throwing and without inserting anything, unlike operator[]), while contains(key) reports presence. Because the reader touches only the keys it names, fields added by a producer are never visited. Protocol Buffers is the alternative whenever the wire format is schema-driven: generated messages ignore fields they do not know and keep them in an UnknownFieldSet across binary round-trips, so old binaries survive new producer fields.
pitfalls: value() returns the default only for a missing key; if the key exists with an incompatible type it throws type_error.302 (the default's type must match the stored value), so a producer-side type change still fails loudly - which is usually what you want, but it must not be mistaken for tolerance of everything.
value() on a non-object throws type_error.306, and nested lookups via JSON pointers throw parse_error.106/109 for malformed indices: each level of navigation needs its own presence or type check.
The default's C++ type determines the return type (j.value("uint64", 0) truncates large unsigned values), so an under-typed default silently corrupts data.

variants.name: Protocol Buffers forward compatibility (unknown fields preserved)
variants.implementation_notes: Here tolerance is a property of the format instead of the reader code: proto3 messages parse fields they do not know into an UnknownFieldSet, re-emit them on serialisation, and let every scalar fall back to its type default, so an old binary keeps working against a newer producer and even forwards fields it cannot interpret. Choose this variant when the wire format is schema-driven (protobuf/Avro-style) and a schema registry governs evolution; note that unknown fields survive binary round-trips but are dropped by JSON/text conversion and by field-by-field copying.
pitfalls: Unknown-field preservation only holds for binary round-trips: converting to/from JSON or copying field-by-field (CopyFrom uses reflection-and-set semantics) drops data the binary never knew about.
proto3 implicit presence cannot distinguish "not set" from "set to the default value": use optional/explicit presence or a wrapper type when absent must be distinguishable from zero or empty.
DiscardUnknownFields() and text-format parsing throw the preserved data away; calling them in a logging or debugging path silently converts a tolerant reader into a lossy one.
